scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

First, the setup: They ordered food through an app, which uses third-party delivery drivers. The payment is done online, and upon delivery, the customer gives the driver a code to get paid. There's a time limit for delivery, and if the driver misses it, they get penalized. Drivers can take multiple orders, but if they take too many, they might not make it on time. In this case, the customer ordered one tea and two pastries but only received one. The shop manager apologized and offered to send the missing pastry. The shop covered the delivery fee, and the customer was given a code to give to the driver upon delivery. Twenty minutes later, the driver called, saying he was on his way. The customer told him they'd give the code when the food arrived. The driver called back a couple more times, each time more urgent, saying he was running out of time. The customer stayed firm, saying they'd give the code only upon receiving the food. The driver snapped, and the customer retorted, hanging up. The driver never delivered, and the shop refunded and reported him. The friend accused the customer of being selfish and unkind, saying the driver might not get paid. The customer argued that the driver shouldn't have taken the order if they couldn't deliver on time. So, the question is: Should the customer have given the code to the driver, trusting he'd deliver, or was it right to hold onto it? Let me think about the rules. The system is designed so that the code is given upon delivery. That makes sense because it ensures the customer gets their food. If the customer gives the code before receiving the food, they might not get their order, and the driver could get paid without delivering. So, the customer was following the system's rules. The driver, on the other hand, took the order, knowing the time constraints. If he took too many orders, he might not make it on time. The customer didn't force the driver to take the order; the driver chose to pick it up. So, the responsibility lies with the driver to manage his time and number of orders. The friend's argument is that the customer was unkind by not trusting the driver. But trust isn't really the issue here. The issue is following the established process to ensure both parties are protected. The customer was protecting their own interests by ensuring they received their order before the driver got paid. Additionally, the driver's behavior was unprofessional. He called multiple times, escalated the situation, and snapped at the customer. That's not a good way to handle a difficult situation. The customer handled it as nicely as possible, only getting annoyed when the driver persisted. In the end, the shop refunded the customer and reported the driver, which suggests that the system supports the customer's action. The driver's failure to deliver on time and his unprofessional conduct led to his potential discipline or firing. So, considering all this, the customer did the right thing by not giving the code until the food was delivered. They followed the system's rules, protected their own interests, and the driver's actions were the cause of his own problem.
